summary: Describes an abstract API to the transport layer, letting protocols and network paths be chosen at runtime. It follows the Transport Services Architecture and provides asynchronous, atomic transmission of Messages, so new protocols can deploy without changing applications.

eli5.summary: Instead of picking a delivery company, you hand over your package and say how fast. The system picks one. This defines the instructions.

how do you clone a connection in transport services
subtitle: The abstract API that lets applications state what they need from the network and leaves protocol and path choice to the system.

tldr.problem: Applications bound to one protocol at compile time cannot benefit from new transport protocols, multiple paths or racing without being rewritten.
tldr.mechanism: The API defines Preconnections, Connections, Listeners, Properties and Messages. Applications set Selection, Connection and Message Properties, call Initiate, Listen or Rendezvous, then send and receive Messages through asynchronous events.
tldr.outcome: New protocols and features can be adopted without changing applications. The document is language-independent and abstract, and is intended to replace the BSD Socket API as the common interface to the transport layer.

today: RFC 9622 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2025 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It is the API that follows the architecture in RFC 9621, with implementation guidance in RFC 9623.

sections.title: Purpose of the API
sections.content:
This document specifies the abstract API that is the interface part of the Transport Services Architecture of RFC 9621. A Transport Services System supports asynchronous, atomic transmission of Messages over transport protocols and network paths chosen dynamically at runtime.

The API lets an implementation pick a transport protocol dynamically instead of binding an application to one at compile time. It also lets an application override the choice and instantiate a specific stack, for example a server that must listen for one protocol. That is discouraged for general use because it can reduce portability.

The API is described in terms of objects, actions, events and parameters. It is language- and platform-independent, so implementations are told to keep the names and the overall shape of the API but may follow local conventions. A non-prescriptive implementation guide is RFC 9623.
sections.eli5: This is a menu that works in every restaurant. How the kitchen cooks is up to the kitchen.

sections.title: Design Principles and Usage
sections.content:
The API offers transport protocols independent of the stacks used at runtime, one API for datagram and stream transports, and Message orientation using application-assisted framing where the transport has none. Establishment, sending and receiving are asynchronous. It supports path selection, transport-specific features, security as a first-order feature, and multistreaming and multipath through Connection Groups.

An application mostly uses two objects. A Preconnection holds Properties and constraints. A Connection is an instance of a transport Protocol Stack, presented consistently whether the transport is connectionless or connection oriented. A Connection comes from one of three actions: Initiate (client), Listen (server) or Rendezvous (peer-to-peer).

The RFC walks through a server that listens and answers, a client that opens a Connection, clones it and sends a request on each, and a peer that resolves local candidates, exchanges them over a signaling channel and rendezvouses. A Preconnection is a template and can be reused after creating a Connection.
sections.eli5: You fill in a request form once. Then you can use it to call someone, wait for calls, or call each other at the same time, and reuse the form later.

sections.title: Specifying Endpoints
sections.content:
Local and Remote Endpoint objects describe the identity of a host and can be more or less specific. An Endpoint can be configured with a host name, a port (a 16-bit unsigned integer), a service name, an IP address, or an interface identifier. An Endpoint MUST NOT carry two identifiers of the same type, so two IP addresses mean two Endpoint objects. Applications should give fully qualified domain names for host names.

A Preconnection used to Listen needs at least one Local Endpoint. One used to Initiate needs at least one Remote Endpoint. Rendezvous needs both. With several Remote Endpoints, the application says they offer an equivalent service and any may be used. An Endpoint can also be tied to a protocol, for instance an alternate port when QUIC is chosen instead of TCP.

Multicast uses separate specifier calls. Initiate gives a send-only Connection to a group, Listen joins a group and creates one Connection per sender, and Rendezvous on an any-source group does both. Rendezvous with a source-specific group as the local identifier is an error.
sections.eli5: An address can be as vague as a street name or as exact as a house number. You can also give several addresses for the same shop, and the system tries them.

sections.title: Transport Properties
sections.content:
Properties come in three kinds. Selection Properties can only be set before establishment and say which paths and stacks are allowed or preferred; afterwards they are read-only. Connection Properties inform establishment and tune the Connection and can be changed later. Message Properties affect individual Messages, and values set on a Preconnection or Connection act as defaults. Setting Connection and Message Properties early is preferred, because they then feed the selection process.

Most Selection Properties use a Preference with five values: Require, Prefer, No Preference, Avoid and Prohibit. The implementation MUST be consistent with Require and Prohibit, while Prefer and Avoid only influence choices. If path and protocol preferences conflict, the path is decided first, since the network path often determines cost to the user.

Examples and defaults include reliability (Require), preserveOrder (Require), preserveMsgBoundaries (No Preference), congestionControl (Require), multistreaming (Prefer), and multipath (Disabled for Initiate and Rendezvous, Passive for Listeners). The defaults represent what can be implemented over TCP. Protocol-specific properties use the protocol acronym as namespace, such as tcp.userTimeoutValue, and vendor ones start with an underscore.

Security Parameters cover allowed security protocols, certificates, pinned server certificates, ALPN, ciphersuites, session cache options, pre-shared keys and callbacks for trust verification and identity challenges.
sections.eli5: You tell the system what you must have, what you would like, and what you want to avoid. It picks the best way that follows your rules.

sections.title: Establishing and Managing Connections
sections.content:
All properties and security parameters must be set before establishment, because they select candidate paths and stacks. After Initiate, changes to the Preconnection have no effect on the Connection. A Ready event arrives once at least one usable stack over one path is established, and no Receive events come before it. An EstablishmentError follows if constraints cannot be met, a name cannot be resolved, or no connection can be made.

Listen returns a Listener that delivers a ConnectionReceived event per new Connection. SetNewConnectionLimit can cap deliveries so a server is not drained of resources, and Stop ends listening. Rendezvous listens and connects simultaneously. The Resolve action can discover NAT bindings (using STUN or TURN) so local candidates can be passed to the peer over a signaling channel, and the implementation then probes reachability as ICE does. Success is reported as RendezvousDone.

Clone creates a Connection Group. Members share all Connection Properties except connPriority, and the shared properties are entangled: changing one on one member changes it on all. A CloneError says a Connection has left its group. AddRemote and RemoveRemote (and local equivalents) change the endpoints of a Connection, for example with Trickle ICE. Generic Connection Properties include connTimeout, keepAliveTimeout, connScheduler, multipathPolicy and groupConnLimit.
sections.eli5: Cloning a connection is like opening extra lanes on the same road. All lanes follow the same rules, except each can have its own priority.

sections.title: Messages, Framers and Data Transfer
sections.content:
Data moves as Messages, each with an optional MessageContext that carries Message Properties, framing metadata and endpoint information. Send is asynchronous, and exactly one of Sent, Expired or SendError is delivered for each call. A Message too large for the stack, such as a datagram larger than the available size, fails with SendError; sendMsgMaxLen reports the limit. An endOfMessage flag supports sending a Message in partial pieces.

Message Properties include msgLifetime (default infinite), msgPriority (default 100, lower number is higher priority), msgOrdered, safelyReplayable, final, msgChecksumLen and msgReliable. Per-Message values can override Connection values where the stack supports it. A Message marked final is sorted to the end, and sending after it causes a SendError.

Message Framers extend the stack to encode outbound Messages and decode inbound data into Messages over byte-stream transports like TCP. They must be added to the Preconnection before any Connection is created, and several Framers form a stack. Receiving is also asynchronous: Receive is paired with a Received event, and partial Messages can be delivered.
sections.eli5: A framer is a person who puts your words into envelopes, so the other side knows where each letter ends even when everything comes in one long strip of paper.

sections.title: Termination and Connection States
sections.content:
A Connection ends by a local action, a remote action or an error such as a timeout. Close finishes after the delivery requirements for Messages already handed over are met and then sends Closed. Abort ends it without delivering remaining Messages and reports a ConnectionError with local Abort as the reason. CloseGroup and AbortGroup do the same for every Connection in the group. Remote termination signals are not guaranteed, so applications should free resources with their own local calls.

A Connection moves from Establishing to Established, then Closing and Closed, with events marking the transitions: Ready, ConnectionReceived or RendezvousDone on entering Established, Closed or ConnectionError on closing, and EstablishmentError if establishment fails. The API guarantees that Sent events follow send order, that Received events never precede establishment, and that no events occur after a Connection is closed.
sections.eli5: Closing is hanging up politely after everything has been said. Aborting is hanging up at once, even if you were mid-sentence.

sections.title: Privacy and Security Considerations
sections.content:
The API configures transport security but does not recommend any particular protocol or algorithm. General requirements, including those about keying material, are in RFC 9621. The implementation is expected to be a trusted library or part of the operating system, and since it handles all network communication, it could share application-provided information with the network or a peer.

One communication attempt can lead to several connection attempts, for example through name resolution, TURN or ICE, racing, or fallback. Early data (0-RTT) sent across multiple paths could reveal information that correlates endpoints. Partial Messages could be a source of truncation attacks if applications do not tell them from complete ones. Early name binding reduces latency but may leak interest if queries are not confidentiality-protected.

Applications can limit protocol and path selection to a small controlled set, and can inspect Connection Properties to see what is in use. A system SHOULD provide a facility logging the communication events of each Connection. There are no IANA actions, though future work might create registries for property names and namespaces.
sections.eli5: Because the system makes many choices for you, you should be able to look at what it chose, and you should handle half-delivered messages with care.

items.label: Require
items.desc: Select only protocols and paths providing the Property; otherwise fail.

items.label: Prefer
items.desc: Prefer protocols and paths providing the Property; otherwise proceed.

items.label: Avoid
items.desc: Prefer protocols and paths not providing the Property; otherwise proceed.

items.label: Prohibit
items.desc: Select only protocols and paths not providing the Property; otherwise fail.
